[0] [0] Apple has submitted a proposal for the fees it can charge for transactions that bypass the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Here's what was included.

[1] [1] Apple Submits Proposal for App Store Bypass Commission

[2] [2] After numerous requests to stay proceedings in district court to determine how much (or even whether) Apple can charge for transactions that bypass the App Store in-app purchase (IAP) system, Apple has finally submitted its proposal into the record, laying out a suggested fee structure.

[3] [3] Apple's submission comes just as the Supreme Court denied its request to stay lower court proceedings while it reviews whether Apple should be held in contempt for charging a 27% commission on transactions that bypass the App Store, allegedly in violation of a court order. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers previously issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to other payment methods.

[4] [4] Apple had argued to the lower court, and then the Supreme Court, that the Supreme Court's decision could impact the outcome of the proceedings to determine fees, so those proceedings should be stayed until the Supreme Court ruled. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing lower court proceedings to continue while it reviews the case.

[5] [5] As a result, Apple's current submission proposes the following fees:

[6] [6] 15% for standard apps, where the current IAP commission rate is 30%; 10% for Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals; 5% for apps under the Small Business Program.

[7] [10] Apple says, "The factual and expert evidence supporting these proposed commission rates has been submitted concurrently." The company adds:

[8] [11] Apple adds that their "proposed external link commission rates are also comparable to commission rates of other similar app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

[9] [12] The company also mentions that "Google Play Store's external link fee is 20% standard, 15% program, 10% subscriptions—rates Epic has already agreed to."

[10] [13] Apple says it still believes that proceedings to determine rates should be stayed while the Supreme Court reviews the case, and that this submission is only to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

[11] [14] The company also points out that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket prohibition on collecting commission on external link transactions, finding that such commissions are only problematic if they effectively amount to a deterrence.

[12] [15] With the proposal submitted into the record, Epic will have a chance to respond, and Apple expects to submit its arguments to the Supreme Court by September 14.
